title: p99-p95 latency deep dive with Hera Robotics
next_steps: Redwood to run benchmark with Hera's 4k-token chat workload and share p95/p99 report by 2027-11-16
Send SOC2 + security pack and on-prem network checklist by 2027-11-12
Schedule design session for Private/VPC deployment (week of 2027-11-20)
Provide preliminary cost vs latency analysis for Dedicated vs Hosted by 2027-11-15
action_items: Maya: send benchmark spreadsheet link and sample prompts by 2027-11-10
Jonas: prepare quantization/kv-cache explanation doc and recommend kernel knobs by 2027-11-12
Priya: share network topology diagram and egress constraints by 2027-11-11
transcript: [00:00] Maya: ok everyone thanks for joining, this is Maya from Redwood, i'm the account lead. we got Jonas with me, our se, who's going to go deep on latency and tail behaviour
[00:08] Liam: hey thanks, excited — we've been hitting some bad p99 spikes on our production agent, so hoping to understand root causes and options
[00:14] Priya: yes we see occasional 2-3x spikes on p99 versus p95, usually during longer conversations and when our frontend streams responses
[00:22] Jonas: great, that's exactly the pattern we see in lots of robotics control loops — streaming versus non-streaming and KV cache misses are typical culprits

[00:30] Diego: quick context — our typical token budget per user is ~4k tokens, models are a 13B open checkpoint, quantized to 4-bit in some envs, and infra is a mix of Dedicated and some self-hosted edge boxes

[00:42] Jonas: thanks diego. let's start with a quick agenda: 1) measurement — how you're measuring p95/p99 and what traces you have, 2) runtime causes — batching, kv cache, quantization impact, 3) network and streaming factors — hops, buffering, websocket vs http2, 4) mitigations and config knobs
[01:00] Maya: also, please call out any compliance constraints for private deploy — priya?
[01:06] Priya: yep SOC2 + in-region data residency, we want optional-private (VPC) with customer KMS. also low egress is important — can't burst a ton to hosted endpoints
[01:20] Jonas: noted — we'll flag network egress tradeoffs between Hosted + Dedicated vs Private. ok measurement first: how are you calculating p95/p99?

[01:28] Liam: currently we compute token-complete latency at the service edge (our API gateway) — includes network to model, model time, and streaming flushes. we use histograms from our sidecar and primarly look at 99th-percentile over 5-minute windows
[01:40] Jonas: good, that includes end-to-end. one trap — if you measure at the edge and there's buffering in the frontend or proxy, you can get inflated p99s that aren't pure model latency
[01:50] Diego: we suspect streaming is amplifying it — sometimes the model returns first few tokens quickly but later tokens stall when kv-cache is garbage-collected or there's a recompile event

[02:00] Jonas: yeah, recompile/debug — that's usually JIT or kernel selection thrash. Redwood's runtime does kernel selection based on sequence-length distribution; long sequences trigger different kernels which can cause a one-off spike if not warmed

[02:12] Jonas: for p99 specifically, the common causes we see are: cold KV-cache (misses on long prefixes), batching variability and head-of-line blocking, kernel recompile / memory pressure, and network/transport stalls
[02:26] Maya: we'll go through each. batching first — priya, how do you batch on the request side? are you doing per-user single requests or multiplexing many users per GPU?

[02:34] Priya: we have a queuing layer that batches up to 8 requests per GPU, but it's adaptive — if latency SLO is tight we lower to 2-4. sometimes we see one request with a huge context blocking the batch

[02:46] Jonas: that's classic head-of-line. Redwood supports continuous batching where long-seq requests can be routed to a slow-path and not block fast-path. we also have per-priority lanes — you can pin low-latency routes with smaller batch sizes and higher priority
[03:00] Liam: can you quantify tradeoffs? like what's the p95 improvement vs cost impact if we separate lanes?

[03:06] Jonas: rough ballpark: isolating a low-latency lane (batch=1-2) typically moves p95 down 20-40% and p99 down more, but throughput drops and unit cost increases ~15-35% depending on GPU utilization and workload mix
[03:18] Diego: and KV-cache? we rely on prefix caching for dialogue state. are misses expensive?

[03:24] Jonas: yes — if the runtime has to rebuild KV cache from scratch per request, you'll pay the full past-context decoding cost. warm caches give huge wins for tail — p99 can go from 1.8s to 250ms for short continuation ops, depending on model and sequence length
[03:38] Jonas: the intervention is to enable persistent KV pools for sticky sessions or use an LRU-backed in-GPU KV with eviction thresholds tuned to your conversation distribution
[03:46] Priya: what's the memory overhead for persistent kv? on our Ded clusters we have mixed tenancy, worried about GPU memory pressure

[03:54] Jonas: depends on model size and max seq length; for 13B with 4k context, persistent KV per active session can be tens to low hundreds of MB. Redwood allows configurable per-model kv budget and also offloads cold kv to host memory with async prefetching to reduce pressure
[04:08] Maya: note that quantization interacts here — diego you mentioned 4-bit. quantization reduces memory but sometimes increases compute jitter?

[04:16] Jonas: correct. 4-bit quantization reduces memory and can reduce per-token latency, but the kernel execution patterns change. some quantized kernels have less consistent tail behaviour, especially on older GPUs or when mixed-precision paths are triggered
[04:28] Jonas: recommended approach: run A/B with both quantized and FP16 on a replay corpus — Redwood's Optimize can suggest quantization profiles and estimate p95/p99 variance
[04:38] Liam: streaming vs non-streaming — we use streaming websockets for UX. are there network-level tricks to reduce tail?

[04:44] Jonas: streaming adds variability because of chunking and network buffering. key things: 1) use smaller flush intervals for interactive flows, 2) avoid proxy buffering (nginx proxy_buffering off), 3) monitor websocket p99 independent of model p99, 4) co-locate edge gateways near GPUs to reduce hops
[05:00] Priya: we do have an internal edge in eu-west-1 and GPUs in the same region, but traffic goes through corporate proxy that does TLS inspection — that adds unpredictable 50-200ms sometimes

[05:10] Jonas: TLS inspection and deep packet inspection are frequent culprits for intermittent tail latency. for Private/VPC deployment you can keep TLS termination inside the VPC and bypass corp proxies — that usually tightens p99
[05:20] Diego: network hops — how many hops is too many? we currently have client -> corp-proxy -> edge gateway -> model cluster -> s3 for context -> cluster

[05:30] Jonas: that's quite a few. each hop can add queuing and variability. aim to minimize cross-az and cross-region hops for latency critical flows. also cache context near the model (local ephemeral store) to avoid s3 round-trips during inference
[05:42] Maya: had a question from procurement — dedicated vs hosted for our case: we want predictable p99 but low egress. what's recommended?

[05:50] Jonas: Dedicated gives predictable throughput and better isolation for KV/persistent caches — usually better p99. Private/on-prem eliminates corp proxies but adds operational complexity. Hosted is easiest but depends on region and network path for egress
[06:00] Jonas: cost vs p99: Dedicated/Private can lower tail by removing noisy neighbors and caching better, but you pay for reserved capacity and potentially engineering ops
[06:08] Liam: you mentioned recompile events earlier — how often do those happen? we've seen sporadic stalls that align with model version rollouts

[06:14] Jonas: recompile or kernel selection thrash usually occurs on first N requests after model load or when sequence-length distribution changes. Redwood uses a lightweight warmup pattern and can precompile common kernel paths during deploy to avoid first-request spikes
[06:28] Jonas: also, auto-scaling events that add new nodes can create redistribution of KV and cause transient p99 blips — recommended to do staggered scaling with warm padding
[06:38] Diego: is there visibility we can add from our side to triage p99? traces?

[06:42] Jonas: yes, instrument token-level timestamps: request in, model accept, token1 out, tokenN out, stream flushes. Redwood's tracing can emit these with per-token timings and tag whether kv hit/miss, batch size, lane used
[06:54] Priya: do you have examples of p95/p99 dashboards we can look at?
[06:58] Maya: we'll share a sample dashboard link — noted in next steps. also we'll include a benchmark spreadsheet template

[07:06] Jonas: let's walk through a few concrete scenarios: scenario A: many short chats (<=512 tokens) mixed with long-running 4k chats — if not isolated, long chats will create tail. mitigations: separate lanes, sticky sessions for kv, session eviction policy tuned to active concurrency
[07:24] Jonas: scenario B: quantized models on mixed hardware — if you see occasional jitter when GPU enters different power states, use pinning and dedicated node pools for quantized workloads
[07:36] Liam: what's the recommended session eviction policy? LRU with time-based TTL?

[07:40] Jonas: typically LRU + TTL with a soft limit works best — e.g., keep 95th percentile of active sessions in-GPU and offload the rest, plus async prefetch for sessions predicted to be reused soon
[07:52] Diego: any tips for model prompt engineering to reduce kv churn? we do a lot of repeat system prompts plus long histories

[07:58] Jonas: compress repeated system prompts into shorter deltas, use embeddings to store long-term memory off-model and only inject short summaries into context — that reduces KV size and speeds cache warming
[08:08] Priya: on the Private/VPC side, any special network requirements? we have strict firewalling

[08:12] Jonas: typical requirements: open egress to Redwood control plane for management (if using Redwood Private), or run full air-gapped stack for on-prem. Port 443 for control plane, but you can do bring-your-own-KMS and SAML SSO. we'll share the network checklist

[08:24] Maya: quick note — if you go air-gapped, you lose some telemetry we use for Optimize recommendations; we can provide local agents that forward minimal metrics to an S3 bucket for analysis rather than full telemetry
[08:36] Liam: interesting. back to measurements — can you help us run a replay benchmark that includes websocket streaming behavior?

[08:42] Jonas: yes — Redwood's bench harness can replay streaming sessions and measure token-level p95/p99 and also simulate corp-proxy delays to model real-world jitter. we'll run with your 4k workload
[08:52] Diego: also want to test quantized vs fp16 and Dedicated vs Hosted — can you simulate capacity constraints?
[08:58] Jonas: we can. we'll run four permutations: (Hosted FP16, Hosted 4-bit, Dedicated FP16, Dedicated 4-bit) and report p50/p95/p99, also memory pressure and recompile counts
[09:10] Priya: that would be great. about streaming flush intervals — what defaults do you recommend?
[09:16] Jonas: interactive flows: 25-50ms flush for first-token latency, then adaptively 100-200ms for subsequent tokens; for very chatty UIs you can push to 30ms but watch network and CPU overhead
[09:30] Maya: circling back to head-of-line blocking — we support priority queues and preemption on Dedicated, is that correct?
[09:36] Jonas: yes, preemption can evict low-priority batches to make room for high-priority single-request lanes. preemption adds some complexity but helps p99 for latency-sensitive routes
[09:46] Liam: any gotchas with preemption and KV consistency?

[09:50] Jonas: if you preempt mid-inference you might need to persist partial KV state or restart that session on the next available lane; Redwood's runtime can save incremental KV snapshots to resume without full rebuild
[10:02] Diego: you mentioned kernel selection — can we pin kernels to avoid on-the-fly recompiles?

[10:06] Jonas: you can pre-warm by running representative sequences during deployment and lock kernel selection for critical models. Redwood also keeps warm caches of compiled kernels per model variant
[10:16] Priya: about monitoring — what alerts should we set for tail detection?

[10:20] Jonas: set alerts on delta between p95 and p99 (e.g., if p99 > p95 * 3), sudden increases in recompile count, kv-miss-rate > X (configurable), and streaming jitter metric — % tokens with inter-token delay > 200ms
[10:34] Liam: ok good. another concern — our edge boxes sometimes have mixed CPU loads causing jitter, is it better to run only lightweight proxies at edge and do heavy work in cloud?

[10:44] Jonas: yes keep edge boxes minimal for proxying and websocket termination; do inference on dedicated GPU pools. moving heavy disk I/O off edge reduces sudden garbage collection that spikes latency
[10:56] Diego: for our benchmark, what traces do you need from us? we can provide per-request logs and network captures

[11:02] Jonas: ideal: sample of real sessions (anonymized), network latency distributions (edge->cluster), proxy config, and representative prompts. we'll also need model config (seq length, quantization bits) and concurrency targets
[11:12] Maya: we'll share the spreadsheet template; diego can drop sample session ids and anonymized traces
[11:18] Priya: security questions — can the runtime encrypt KV in GPU memory or is it plaintext?

[11:24] Jonas: GPUs don't natively do full-playground KMS; KV in GPU memory is not encrypted at rest but the host can encrypt saved snapshots with customer KMS before persisting. for Private on-prem we support HSM integration for key wrapping
[11:36] Liam: OK. any performance penalty for encrypting snapshots?

[11:40] Jonas: minimal for async saves — the encrypt happens on host CPU but it's done off the critical path; restoring does add a bit of latency if you need to decrypt synchronously, so we recommend async restores and warm prefetch
[11:52] Diego: let's talk about scheduling — if we want a predictable p99 for 99.9% of requests, what headroom do we reserve?

[11:58] Jonas: industry practice is to provision 20-30% headroom for Dedicated, and for strict SLOs consider dedicated low-latency pools sized for peak concurrency. autoscaling must be warm-aware — keep min nodes warm
[12:10] Liam: earlier you mentioned prefetch — what's the logic for prefetching KV? how do you predict reuse?
[12:16] Jonas: simple heuristics: sticky sessions, last-recently-used plus ML-based predictors using user activity; Redwood Optimize can suggest thresholds from historical traces
[12:28] Maya: quick check — are there any features we should enable now to immediately reduce p99?

[12:34] Jonas: yes: enable persistent KV for active sessions, create a low-latency lane for interactive users, disable proxy buffering, and pre-warm kernels during deploy. those typically show immediate improvements
[12:46] Priya: sounds actionable. about deployment: if we choose Private/VPC, does Redwood still manage updates?

[12:52] Jonas: for Redwood Private we offer a control plane integration — you can choose managed updates or self-managed; managed updates let us push kernel precompiles and runtime patches with your approval
[13:04] Diego: any recommended observability tags to put into our logs? session id, kv-hit, batch-size, lane-id, kernel-version?
[13:12] Jonas: exactly. include token timestamps, kv_hit boolean, batch_size, lane_id, kernel_sig, and node_id so we can correlate spikes to specific nodes or kernel versions
[13:24] Liam: can you show an example trace where kv-miss caused a p99 blip?
[13:28] Jonas: yes i have a short snippet — (Jonas screenshare) — here's a trace: tokens 1-40 fast, then 1.8s gap while KV rebuilt, then resume. tagged as kv_miss=true, batch_size=1, lane=low-prio
[13:42] Maya: note: we'll attach that example trace in the follow-up email
[13:48] Priya: one more procurement-y Q: if we pick Dedicated, can we burst to Hosted in overflow?

[13:54] Jonas: yes, Redwood supports policy-based routing: burst to Hosted or lower-tier models when Dedicated is saturated. with automatic fallback you sacrifice some latency predictability but preserve availability
[14:06] Diego: about lower-tier models — are there quantized model variants that are faster but still acceptable quality?

[14:10] Jonas: yes, we provide curated model variants with quantization profiles and quality regressions measured against eval sets. Optimize will recommend the model with best cost/latency/quality tradeoff for your workload
[14:22] Maya: okay we're ~14 minutes in the transcript — want to speed through remaining configs and then capture final decisions
[14:28] Liam: yes let's do that

[14:30] Jonas: summarizing recommended immediate actions: 1) enable persistent KV, 2) create low-latency lane and priority preemption, 3) disable proxy buffering, 4) pre-warm kernels on deploy, 5) run the benchmark permutations (Hosted/Dedicated x FP16/4-bit)
[14:44] Priya: agreed. a couple of constraints: we need in-region Private due to data residency, and limited egress — can Redwood's Private run fully within our VPC?
[14:52] Jonas: yes, Redwood Private can run with a customer-managed control plane in your VPC; we support BYO-KMS and SAML SSO. we'll include the network checklist
[14:58] Diego: any latency hit from BYO-KMS?
[15:02] Jonas: negligible for runtime since KMS used only for snapshot encryption and occasional auth; critical path is mostly network and model compute, not KMS
[15:10] Liam: great. one operational ask: if tail spikes happen during business hours, we want automatic escalation — can Redwood hook into our incident channels?
[15:18] Maya: yes we can integrate with pager duty/slack and push alerts based on the p99 thresholds you set
[15:24] Priya: ok after the benchmark, who owns the validation?
[15:28] Jonas: Redwood will run the bench and provide raw traces; your eng team validates on their side and we do a joint post-mortem on any discrepancies
[15:36] Diego: timeline question — how long to run full permutations?
[15:40] Jonas: about 4-5 days end-to-end to provision nodes, run tests at different concurrencies, and analyze. quicker if we start with smaller sample size
[15:48] Maya: we'll propose dates in follow-up. moving to Q&A — Priya had a deep network question earlier?
[15:54] Priya: yes two quick things: 1) for corp proxy bypass we need a design that still meets compliance, 2) we'd like a formal SLA for p99 if we go Dedicated
[16:04] Jonas: for proxy bypass we recommend an internal-only endpoint that terminates TLS within VPC; for SLA we offer enterprise SLAs on Dedicated contracts — we'll have sales draft that
[16:12] Liam: ok let's recap next steps

[16:16] Maya: recap: - Redwood to run benchmark (Hosted/Dedicated x FP16/4-bit) with Hera's 4k token workload; - send SOC2/security pack; - share dashboard + example traces; - schedule Private design call; - provide cost vs latency spreadsheet
[16:32] Priya: sounds good. Diego will upload sample sessions and network captures to the spreadsheet
[16:38] Diego: will do by EOD tomorrow
[16:40] Liam: thanks everyone, very helpful session
[16:42] Maya: thanks all — we'll follow up with a summary email and items. bye
[16:45] (call ended)
